strengths: Proposes MVAR, a next-scale autoregressive framework that uses scale and spatial Markov assumptions to reduce redundancy in VAR-style models, with clear motivation from attention-weight analyses.

Achieves substantial efficiency gains: eliminates KV cache, reduces attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), and lowers inference memory by about 3-4.2x while enabling training on eight RTX 4090 GPUs.

Reports improved FID and IS over VAR on ImageNet 256x256 for both a 310M model trained from scratch and fine-tuned larger models, with standard generative metrics and ablations on scale conditioning and neighborhood size.
Provides complexity analysis and detailed implementation hyperparameters, making the approach relatively reproducible.
The paper is generally well organized and the visualizations help communicate the core ideas.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method combines known ideas (Markovian conditioning, local/neighborhood attention) with VAR, and the key observations are post-hoc attention statistics from pretrained VAR models rather than rigorous theoretical guarantees.

The technical formulation is unclear and possibly inconsistent: Eq. 3-7 appear to define Q, K, V from the same scale, whereas the method claims conditioning on the adjacent scale; the definition of a 'corresponding' neighborhood across different-resolution scales is vague, and the exact implementation is not specified.

Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; no high-resolution, text-to-image, or video experiments are provided, and important recent efficient VAR variants (e.g., HART, Infinity, FastVAR, Collaborative Decoding) are cited but not empirically compared.

The main comparison may not be fully controlled: MVAR is trained from scratch while VAR is evaluated with official pretrained weights; the fine-tuning comparison improves FID/IS but some metrics such as recall decrease, and no multiple seeds or statistical significance tests are reported.

Ablation studies use a shorter 50-epoch schedule, so it is unclear whether the conclusions hold under full training; the causal-masking strategy for the final two scales is unusual and insufficiently explained.
The approach still relies on the original VQ-VAE tokenizer from VAR, and broader ethical considerations of high-fidelity image generation (e.g., potential misuse) are not discussed.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated by observed redundancy in VAR attention patterns, and the proposed scale-Markov plus spatial-Markov conditioning is intuitive and easy to follow.
The efficiency direction is practically relevant: reducing training/inference memory and removing the growing multi-scale KV cache would be valuable for visual autoregressive models.

The manuscript reports ImageNet 256x256 experiments with FID/IS/Precision/Recall, includes ablations on scale conditioning and neighborhood size, and shows modest improvements over VAR on several metrics.
The writing and figures are generally clear, and the method description provides sufficient high-level intuition to understand the intended efficiency gains.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: conditioning only on the adjacent scale and using local/window attention are straightforward simplifications of existing next-scale AR models, closely related to prior work on efficient/local attention and autoregressive visual generation. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution from existing approaches such as local neighborhood attention or coarse-to-fine efficient AR variants.

The comparative evaluation in Table 2 is not apples-to-apples: pretrained VAR models are compared against fine-tuned MVAR variants, which can trivially improve metrics due to additional fine-tuning. A fine-tuned VAR baseline under the same schedule is missing, so the claimed gains are unsupported.

The main results table omits several recent and strong autoregressive image-generation baselines (e.g., MAR, RAR, HART, Infinity), making the empirical positioning incomplete. Evaluation is also limited to ImageNet 256x256, with no 512x512 or text-to-image experiments.

There are hardware/memory inconsistencies: reported inference and training memory values (e.g., 40,971 MB, 34,319 MB, 38,579 MB) exceed the 24 GB capacity of a single RTX 4090, yet the captions state experiments were conducted on an RTX 4090. It is unclear whether these are aggregate multi-GPU numbers, and this ambiguity undermines the central memory-reduction claims.

Several technical details are unclear or inconsistent. Eq. (5) defines attention using K^l and V^l from the current scale, while the method claims conditioning on the adjacent previous scale r_{l-1}. Eq. (1) appears to define residual quantization with only r_{l-1}, but VAR's tokenizer uses all previous scales r_{<l}; this conflicts with the stated use of the original VAR VQ-VAE. The causal mask for r_9/r_10, where causal masking is disabled, is also unclear and risks future-scale information leakage.

The complexity claims are not fully supported by measurements. Although the paper claims a reduction from O(N^2) to O(Nk), Table 4 shows only about a 19% GFLOP reduction versus the baseline, and the analysis ignores non-attention costs and small-scale cases where k covers the whole scale.

Ablation results are relatively weak and reported for only a 50-epoch schedule without seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance. The observed FID/IS differences may be within noise, making the claimed superiority of the Markovian assumptions uncertain.
Reproducibility is insufficient: no code or model release is mentioned, key tokenizer/training details for the modified attention are missing, and the fine-tuning procedure is not fully specified.

Some claims are overstated: the method is described as outperforming 'nearly all' competing models, but stronger models such as DiT-XL/2 and StyleGAN-XL still achieve better FID in Table 1, and 'eliminating KV cache' is somewhat misleading because the method still requires features from the previous scale during inference.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical observations: attention weights concentrate on adjacent scales and local spatial neighborhoods, which directly motivate the proposed scale- and spatial-Markovian conditioning.

Substantial practical benefits: reduces attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk), removes KV cache during inference, and enables training/fine-tuning on relatively modest hardware (8 RTX 4090s) with strong memory reductions.
The proposed method is simple and effective, achieving better FID/IS than VAR in the main ImageNet 256x256 comparison while preserving comparable precision/recall in several settings.
Ablation studies are informative, covering the number of conditioning scales and the neighborhood size k, and generally support the design choices.
The paper is well organized, with detailed hyperparameters and complexity analysis in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The Markovian assumptions are motivated mainly by attention-weight statistics, but attention concentration does not formally imply conditional independence. The probabilistic justification for discarding non-adjacent scales and non-local tokens is therefore somewhat heuristic.

Novelty is moderate: scale-Markov conditioning essentially truncates the conditioning prefix to the previous scale, and spatial-Markov attention closely resembles existing neighborhood/local attention mechanisms. The contribution is mostly an effective application/combination of known ideas in the next-scale AR setting.

Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256. There are no text-to-image, higher-resolution, video, or other domain experiments, so the generality of the proposed Markovian conditioning remains unclear.

Some results are inconsistent or under-explained: Table 1 reports MVAR-310M FID 3.09, while Table 2 reports fine-tuned MVAR-d16† FID 3.40; training memory values (e.g., 38GB) are ambiguous on RTX 4090 hardware and may be aggregate rather than per-GPU.
Recall sometimes drops relative to VAR (e.g., Table 2 d16: 0.48 vs. 0.51; d20: 0.52 vs. 0.56), suggesting possible diversity loss that is not fully analyzed.
Important implementation details are missing or vague, including how the k-neighborhood is mapped across scales and the exact parallel training masks for scales r1-r8, which may hinder reproduction.
No broader-impact or ethical discussion is provided, despite the method being applicable to image generation with potential misuse concerns.

strengths: Introduces scale-Markov and spatial-Markov conditioning for next-scale visual autoregressive modeling, significantly reducing memory usage (about 3x) and eliminating KV cache during inference.
Provides empirical attention-weight analyses to motivate the Markov assumptions, and the proposed spatial-Markov attention reduces attention complexity from O(N^2) to O(Nk).
Demonstrates practical efficiency benefits, enabling training on eight RTX 4090 GPUs, with strong memory and training-speed improvements over VAR.
Includes experiments on ImageNet 256x256, ImageNet 512x512, CelebA, and FFHQ, plus ablations on conditioning prefix length and neighborhood size k.
The from-scratch MVAR-d16 model improves FID and IS over the VAR-d16 baseline while using less memory.
weaknesses: The core idea is largely a combination of existing techniques: adjacent-scale conditioning (scale-Markov) and local/neighborhood attention, which limits novelty relative to the original VAR contribution.

Large-model results rely on fine-tuned variants (MVAR†) compared against original VAR rather than a fine-tuned VAR baseline under the same schedule, so performance gains may be partially confounded by fine-tuning.

The paper lacks comparisons to other recent efficient next-scale or autoregressive image generation methods (e.g., HART, FastVAR, Infinity) and does not report from-scratch results for larger models due to compute constraints.

Some equations and notations are confusing: Eqs. 5-6 define K^l and V^l at the same scale as Q^l, while the method describes conditioning on the adjacent previous scale; this makes the spatial-Markov attention implementation unclear.
Inference-time improvements are modest (e.g., 0.34s to 0.27s per batch in Table 2) despite large memory savings, so the practical generation-speed benefit is less pronounced than the memory claims.
The motivation from attention weights does not establish that non-adjacent scales are truly redundant; stronger causal validation across datasets and resolutions would be needed.
Reproducibility is partially limited by custom CUDA kernels and a mixed training strategy, with implementation details deferred to the appendix and code not yet released.

strengths: The paper is clearly motivated by visualizations of attention patterns in VAR and proposes a simple, intuitive modification: scale-Markov conditioning and spatial-Markov attention.
The efficiency benefits are practically meaningful: no KV cache during inference, lower GPU memory, and training on eight RTX 4090 GPUs.
The experimental section covers ImageNet 256x256/512x512, CelebA, and FFHQ, with multiple model sizes and both scratch and fine-tuning settings.
The proposed method often improves FID/IS over VAR in the reported settings while reducing memory and GFLOPs.
The paper includes a reproducibility statement and detailed hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: scale-Markov conditioning is essentially truncated autoregressive conditioning, and spatial-Markov attention is closely related to existing local/neighborhood attention mechanisms; the contribution is mainly an engineering combination with VAR.

The central justification relies on attention weights from a pre-trained VAR model. Attention weights alone do not establish conditional independence or redundancy, and removing all non-adjacent scales could discard useful global information. The paper lacks causal interventions or more rigorous analysis to support the Markov assumptions.

There are technical ambiguities in the spatial-Markov attention formulation. Eq. (5)-(7) define Q/K/V from the same token map r_l, while the method is described as attending to adjacent scales. It is unclear how neighborhoods are defined across different resolutions, how token correspondence is handled, and how η_k is computed. The custom CUDA kernels and mixed training strategy are not described in enough detail to reproduce.

The evaluation has a serious confound: MVAR† models are fine-tuned from pre-trained VAR for additional epochs, but the VAR baselines are not given the same fine-tuning protocol. The large-model comparisons therefore do not isolate the effect of the proposed architectural changes. The paper also does not report scratch-trained MVAR-d20/d24 models, despite claiming comparable or superior performance for large models.
The paper does not compare against recent efficient VAR variants such as HART, Infinity, or FastVAR, which are highly relevant baselines for the efficiency claims.

Some reported memory numbers appear inconsistent with the stated hardware: e.g., ImageNet-512 and CelebA tables report 43-46 GB memory on an RTX 4090 (24 GB), which is impossible without further explanation (e.g., CPU offloading or multi-GPU aggregation). This undermines reproducibility.

The claimed O(N^2) to O(Nk) complexity reduction is not convincingly reflected in the measured GFLOPs, which drop only from 43.61 to 35.44 in the main ablation. The ablation on the number of preceding scales is also non-monotonic: 2 and 3 scales are worse than the full baseline, while only 1 scale improves, which weakens the story that removing redundancy generally helps.

The paper contains several clarity and presentation issues: inconsistent notation, missing or unclear definitions, and typos in citations (e.g., 'Brock et al., 1809'). The appendix adds some results but also introduces further inconsistencies and unsupported claims.

The significance of the contribution may be limited for a top-tier AI conference: the method is a combination of existing ideas with moderate empirical gains, and the strongest claims are not fully supported by fair, controlled experiments.

strengths: Targets a real efficiency bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation: memory and KV cache, with a simple and plausible reformation of next-scale prediction.

Scale-Markov conditioning and spatial-Markov attention are well motivated by attention-weight analyses and yield substantial practical gains: ~3x lower memory, no KV cache, O(Nk) attention, training on 8 RTX 4090s.
Empirical results on ImageNet-256 from scratch show MVAR-d16 improves FID/IS over VAR-d16, and ablations isolate benefits of scale and spatial Markovian conditioning and neighborhood size k.
Additional experiments on ImageNet-512, CelebA, FFHQ, and 2B model suggest generalization and scalability.
Paper is generally clear, with useful figures and detailed hyperparameters; code/checkpoints promised.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: spatial-Markov attention is essentially neighborhood/local attention already explored in prior work, and scale-Markov conditioning is a truncation of VAR's context; the core contribution is an application/combination.

Markov assumptions are motivated by averaged attention weights, not formal conditional-independence tests or theory; dropping all non-adjacent scales may discard useful global context, and the justification is empirical/approximate.

Evaluation is not fully apples-to-apples: large-model results in Table 2 fine-tune pretrained VAR into MVAR but do not compare against a VAR baseline fine-tuned for the same schedule; for d20/d24, IS and recall are lower than VAR, so 'comparable or superior' is somewhat overstated.
Main from-scratch result only covers d16; no from-scratch training for larger models due resources, limiting evidence for scalability and architectural superiority.
Missing comparisons to recent efficient visual AR methods (e.g., HART, Infinity, etc.) in the main quantitative table, despite discussing them in related work.
Implementation details of mixed training and custom CUDA kernels for r9/r10 are not fully specified, which may affect reproducibility and practical adoption.
